title: Signature OE3 Loop Design One
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature OE3 loop design one is an original speculative design for a closed energy loop: a store, a converter, a load, and a return path, drawn with an explicit accounting gate that measures energy in and out of every element on every cycle. The design's rule is that the gate's reading decides the loop's status, and no element may skip the gate. The design is labeled speculative because no loop of this kind has demonstrated net gain, and the record claims no gain.

The loop's value as a design is its accounting discipline rather than its mechanism: by forcing every element through one measured gate, it makes hidden inputs visible, which is exactly where past claims have failed. A loop that passes its gate with a balance is a conventional storage loop; a loop that appears to pass only by going around the gate is a failed test, and the design says to report it as such.

The demo simulates ten cycles through a loop with a stated efficiency below unity, printing stored energy as it decays. The simulation demonstrates the accounting rule: with honest losses, the loop runs down. It is not evidence for or against any future mechanism.

Working demo: the record carries a small standard-library program that demonstrates the core mechanism. The demo was executed at build time and its stored output byte-matches a fresh run; it uses no network and no external package.

title: Signature OE3 Loop Design Two
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature OE3 loop design two is an original speculative design that adds a second store to the loop, so energy can rest in one store while the other discharges, smoothing the load's supply. The design's question is whether two stores change anything fundamental, and its own answer is no: stores change timing, not totals, and the accounting gate still decides the loop's status. The design includes the second store to make that point concrete rather than abstract.

Two stores do help a real system in one way: they let the load run steadily while charging happens in bursts, which is useful for intermittent sources. The design distinguishes that genuine benefit, load smoothing, from the speculative benefit, net gain, and it claims only the first. That distinction is the design's honesty mechanism.

The demo alternates two stores across cycles with a stated efficiency, printing each store's level. It is an accounting simulation, not a loop test.

title: Signature Axiom Turbine Design
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature axiom turbine design is an original speculative design built around a small piece of design mathematics: a turbine rule written as a recurrence that holds a value at unity across a range and then follows it beyond that range. The design treats the recurrence as a specification to be tested, not as a proof of anything: it asks what physical turbine, if any, would follow the rule, what its losses would be, and what measurement would show the rule failing. Those questions are the design, and the record gives no performance figure for the turbine.

The design is explicit that mathematics alone does not make a machine: a recurrence on paper costs nothing to run, while a turbine costs energy to build, spin, and maintain, and the two must not be confused. The turbine record therefore pairs every mathematical statement with a physical question about friction, materials, and measurement, and it leaves those questions open.

The demo runs the recurrence over a stated range and prints its values. It is a recurrence illustration, not a turbine test, and it claims no energy result.

title: Signature OE3 Accounting Gate
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature OE3 accounting gate is an original design for a measurement point that every energy element in a loop must pass through: the gate logs energy in, energy out, time, and element identity for each cycle, and it refuses to report a balance for any cycle with a missing log entry. The gate is the design's core invention, not because measurement is novel, but because making measurement unavoidable is what past claims avoided.

The gate's rules are deliberately boring: same units, same cycle boundaries, uncertainties stated, no term labeled negligible without a bound. Boring rules are the point, because exciting rules are how gaps hide. A gate built to those rules can be implemented with ordinary instruments, and the design includes a worked example showing the log format.

The demo implements the gate's balance check on a small cycle log, printing the balance and whether any entry is missing. It is a logging illustration, not a measurement.

title: Signature OE3 Friction Audit
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. The Signature OE3 friction audit is an original design for listing every friction source in a loop before any gain is discussed: bearings, gear meshes, seals, air drag, and electrical resistance, each with a measurement method and an uncertainty. The audit's rule is that an unlisted loss is treated as unknown, not as zero, and the loop's balance is reported as unknown until the audit is complete. That rule alone would have settled most historical claims.

The audit template gives each loss a row, a method, and a bound, and it requires the auditor to sign the completed audit before the loop runs. Signing matters because it makes the audit a commitment rather than a wish list, and a later missing loss can then be traced to a specific row rather than to vague optimism.

The demo totals a small audit table and prints the loss budget. It is a template illustration with assumed values.

The Signature OE3 measurement protocol is an original design for testing any loop in the program: complete cycles starting and ending in the same state, simultaneous measurement of all inputs and outputs, runs long enough for transients to die, independent instruments chosen by the tester, and publication of method and data. The protocol is adapted from standard claim-evaluation practice, and the design credits that practice rather than presenting the protocol as novel.

The protocol's final step, archiving data, is treated as equal in importance to the test itself, because a test whose data cannot be re-examined is only a story. The design specifies a data format, a file layout, and a retention rule, all deliberately simple so that archiving actually happens.

The demo prints the protocol's steps in order. It is a procedure document, not a test result.

title: Signature OE3 Store Design
body:

The Signature OE3 store design is an original design for the loop's energy store: a flywheel-assisted store with a stated capacity, charge rate, and loss rate, chosen so that the store's behavior can be modeled exactly. The design's contribution is not the store itself, which uses conventional components, but the store's specification sheet, which states capacity, losses, and failure modes in the same format as the accounting gate's log, so store and gate speak the same language.

The store's failure modes are specified alongside its capacities: overspeed, bearing wear, and thermal limits, each with a sensor and a shutdown rule. A store without failure modes is a hope, not a component, and the design refuses to describe one.

The demo models the store charging and discharging with a stated efficiency, printing its level over cycles. It is a store model with assumed values.

title: Signature OE3 Converter Design
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature OE3 converter design is an original design for the loop's conversion element, which changes stored energy into the load's required form at a stated efficiency below unity. The design's rule is that efficiency is measured, not assumed: the converter's sheet gives efficiency at five load points, measured under the program's protocol, and any loop calculation must use the measured point nearest its operating load rather than the converter's best point.

Using best-point efficiency everywhere is a common accounting error, because converters are least efficient exactly where loops often operate, at light load. The design's five-point sheet exists to prevent that error, and the loop's balance must be recomputed if the operating point moves.

The demo interpolates converter efficiency at a stated load from a five-point sheet and prints the result. It is an interpolation illustration with assumed sheet values.

title: Signature OE3 Load Design
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature OE3 load design is an original design for the loop's load: a resistive load bank with switched steps, so the loop's output can be measured at known, repeatable loads rather than inferred from a vague application. The load bank's steps are calibrated resistors, and the design gives the calibration method, because an uncalibrated load makes output measurements meaningless.

The load design also specifies a dummy-load procedure: before any loop test, the load bank is driven from a known supply and its measurements are checked against prediction. A load bank that fails its dummy check is repaired before the loop runs, not during it, so that load errors never masquerade as loop behavior.

The demo computes power at three load steps from voltage and resistance, printing each. It is an electrical illustration with assumed values.

title: Signature OE3 Return Path Design
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature OE3 return path design is an original design for the loop's return leg, which carries energy from the load side back toward the store. The design's question is the return leg's efficiency, and its rule is that the return leg is measured separately, under the same protocol as the converter, rather than inferred from the loop's overall behavior. The Signature OE3 cycle simulator is an original design for a teaching program that simulates a loop from its elements' efficiency sheets, so that a designer can see the loop's balance before building anything. The simulator's rule is that it never invents efficiency: every element's efficiency comes from a sheet, and a missing sheet stops the simulation with a plain error naming the element. The Signature OE3 independent test plan is an original design for handing a loop to an outside tester: the tester chooses the instruments, defines the cycle, runs the protocol, and publishes method and data, while the designer answers questions but does not touch the apparatus during the test. The plan's independence rule is absolute during the test window, because a test the designer can influence is a demonstration, not a test.

The plan also specifies the test's stopping rules: how many cycles, what counts as a complete cycle, and what result counts as success, all written before the test starts. Pre-written stopping rules prevent the common failure in which a test runs until a flattering stretch appears and then stops.

title: Signature OE3 Reporting Template

The Signature OE3 reporting template is an original design for reporting loop results: a summary that states what was tested, what was found, and what was not shown, followed by the full energy account, the loss audit, the instrument list, and the raw cycle log. The template's rule is that the summary must not outrun the tables, and any summary sentence that the tables do not support is rewritten, not defended.

The template separates confirmatory results, which tested a pre-written prediction, from exploratory results, which were found by looking at the data, and it labels each accordingly. That separation is what lets a reader trust the confirmatory numbers while still learning from the exploratory ones.

The demo assembles a report skeleton from a trial list and prints the confirmatory and exploratory counts. It is a template, not a report of results.

The Signature OE3 teaching ladder is an original teaching design ordering the program from simple to most-complex: energy accounting first, then loss audits, then loop simulation, then the independent test plan, and finally the honesty statement as the capstone. Each rung states what the learner should be able to do, so the ladder is a progression of skills: balance an account, audit losses, simulate a loop, design a test, and state a position honestly.

The ladder's rule is that no rung's lesson depends on accepting a later rung's speculation: a learner who stops after accounting should still have a complete, correct skill, not a half-finished promise. That independence is what makes the ladder useful as teaching even for readers who never accept any speculative design in the program.
